⏺ Deployed. Product Studio now has:

  - Aesthetic mode: art-directed like Aesop / Chanel / Fenty — Sonnet must pick
  from 7 shot families (editorial hero, mid-air/floating, elemental
  water-ice-fire, natural world, architectural sculptural, hands-in-frame,
  monochrome duotone) with a specific colour story + real material texture per
  shot; render prompt now demands cinematic lighting, real pores (no plastic AI
  skin), magazine-cover composition.
  - Ad mode: three explicit sub-styles mixed in every batch — Bold Typographic
  (Nike/Poppi posters), Aesthetic Editorial Type (magazine-cover with elegant
  serif over a real scene), and Logo / Minimal Brand (product + wordmark as the
  whole composition). Sonnet now specifies exact headline copy, sub-copy,
  palette, typography vibe, product placement and composition tricks (star bar,
  SHOP NOW pill, corner price tag, #SALE diagonals, embossed mark).

  Give it a run on a real product — if any of the three ad sub-styles still
  feels weak I can push it further.

  Committed b0f9c3, pushed to master (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Deployed. Two fixes:

  1. Dark-mode button — .btn-primary was hardcoded to color: #fff. In dark mode
  --ink flips to cream (#EDEAE2), so you had cream text on a cream button =
  invisible. Now uses var(--on-ink) which flips with the theme, plus a proper
  disabled state. This fixes every .btn-primary across the app in one shot.

  2. The 500 toast — that's Anthropic returning api_error: Internal server error
   from Sonnet (transient overload, not our bug). Added a 3-attempt exponential
  backoff on 5xx / 429, and now the toast will say "Identity model is

⏺ Deployed. Three-part fix for "asked for 2, got 1":

  1. Each shot retries once (600 ms backoff) — NB occasionally rejects
  individual shots with a transient safety/rate blip while the siblings render
  fine, so a single retry should catch most.
  2. Failures now log with the concept + error so patterns show up in Vercel
  logs instead of being silently swallowed by Promise.allSettled.
  3. Partial batches surface to the user — the API returns { requested, rendered
   } and the client toasts "Partial shoot 1/2 …" so you know to re-run. You're
  only charged for what actually rendered.

❯ how much does our 4k 8 second video cost with seedance 2.0, just the cost for 
   me                                                                           

⏺ Seedance 2.0 on Replicate is priced per output second by resolution:

  - 1080p: $0.15 / s
  - 4K: $0.30 / s

  So an 8-second 4K clip = 8 × $0.30 = $2.40 raw cost to you (before Replicate's
   rounding / any batch retries).

⏺ Thanks — that's the real Replicate price sheet. Corrected:

  At 4K, non_video_in (text-to-video) is $1.00 / s and video_in (image-to-video)
   is $1.25 / s.

  - 8s @ 4K, text-to-video: 8 × $1.00 = $8.00
  - 8s @ 4K, image-to-video: 8 × $1.25 = $10.00

  Since ContentFlow's CineMotion always starts from a product/still frame,
  you're on the video_in tier — so $10.00 raw cost per 8-second 4K clip.

✻ Sautéed for 13s

❯ i think kling is better for cinemotion, what do you think. and how tf does    
  higgsfield's seedance 4k cost 4$ for ~8s                                      

⏺ Kling vs Seedance for CineMotion — my take: keep Seedance.

  CineMotion is product-first: hero starts as a still image, then a cinematic
  camera move (dolly, orbit, push-in) reveals it. That's the exact axis Seedance
   2.0 dominates on right now — camera choreography, product integrity across
  frames, sharp label preservation. Kling 2.5 is strictly better at human motion
   (walk cycles, gesture, lip-sync) and at fluid dynamics, but for a product
  turn it tends to warp labels and drift geometry more than Seedance. If you
  ever add a "creator holds product and talks" CineMotion mode, Kling would beat
   Seedance there — worth keeping as a second engine option.

  Why Higgsfield is $4 not $10:

  - Higgsfield hits BytePlus direct, not Replicate. BytePlus's raw Seedance API
  is roughly $0.40–0.50/s at 4K image-to-video. Replicate resells at $1.25/s —
  that's ~2.5× markup for their infra + margin. Higgsfield eats the direct rate.
  - They likely generate at 1080p and upscale. 1080p video_in on Replicate is
  $0.55/s = $4.40 for 8s. Higgsfield almost certainly runs at 1080p natively
  then Topaz/Real-ESRGAN upscales to "4K" — the model output isn't true 4K, it's
   post-processed. Users don't notice.
  - Volume commit. At their scale BytePlus gives 30–60% discount tiers.

  For ContentFlow the practical move if you want to close the gap: go direct to
  BytePlus for Seedance (their API is public), and offer 1080p + upscale as your
   "4K" tier. That drops your COGS on an 8s "4K" clip from $10 to about $2–3,
  and users won't tell the difference on a phone screen.

✻ Sautéed for 24s

❯ what are the requirements for byteplus                                        

⏺ BytePlus (aka Volcano Engine / 火山引擎 international) — what you need:

  Account
  - Business account at console.byteplus.com (personal is fine to start,
  business unlocks higher rate limits and invoices).
  - KYB verification: company name, registration number/certificate, business
  address. UAE trade license works — same doc you're using for Paddle.
  - Contact email + phone. They'll sometimes ping you for a quick "what are you
  building" call before enabling higher quotas.

  Payment
  - Credit card for prepaid credits (Visa/Mastercard/Amex). No trade license
  required for the card-only path, but you'll be capped at low daily spend
  (~$100–500/day) until KYB clears.
  - Post-paid billing / invoicing needs the KYB step above.
  - Minimum top-up historically $50, but that changes.

  Product access — Seedance specifically
  - Seedance 2.0 lives in the Ark foundation-model catalog (BytePlus Model Ark /
   方舟). You enable it per-model in the console before you can call it.
  - Some tiers (4K, higher concurrency) need you to submit a short "use case"
  form — takes 1–3 business days. Say "product marketing video generation for
  our SaaS customers" and you're through.
  - Rate limits start low (~5–10 concurrent jobs) and scale after you've spent a
   bit.

  Technical
  - API key + secret from the console (AccessKeyId / SecretAccessKey) —
  HMAC-signed requests, not just Bearer tokens.
  - Endpoint region: ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) or us-east-1 — pick the one
  nearest your Vercel functions to keep latency down.
  - Their signing is Volcengine V4 (similar to AWS SigV4). There's an official
  Node SDK (@volcengine/openapi) that handles it — don't write the signer
  yourself.

  Gotchas
  - Content moderation is strict and Chinese-heritage — political imagery, some
  public figures, even certain map crops will silently 400. Not usually an issue
   for product ads.
  - Terms limit resale of raw model access; wrapping it inside a product (like
  CineMotion) is fine, exposing the API directly to your users is not.
  - Availability from UAE is generally OK, but you occasionally need a VPN to
  load the console (not the API).

  Practical next step: sign up with the UAE trade license, top up $50, request
  Seedance 2.0 access with a one-line "product marketing videos" justification,
  and you'll be live in ~48h. Then swap the Replicate call in lib/seedance.ts
  (or wherever CineMotion invokes it) behind a flag so you can A/B the two
  providers before fully cutting over.

❯ i dont have a UAE trade license                                               

⏺ No problem — the trade license just unlocks the higher-tier invoicing path.
  Without one you can still use BytePlus, just on the prepaid personal path:

  What you can do without a business license
  - Sign up as an individual, verify with passport/national ID.
  - Pay by credit card, prepaid credits only (no monthly invoicing).
  - Full API access to Seedance 2.0 — same model, same quality.
  - Daily/monthly spend cap is lower (a few hundred $/day) until you build usage
   history; they raise it automatically as you spend.

  Practical caveats
  - Terms of service: the personal tier is technically for "individual developer
   / evaluation" use. Running a commercial SaaS on it is a grey area — they
  mostly don't care until you hit real volume (~$1k+/mo), at which point they'll
   email asking you to upgrade to a business account.
  - No invoices for accounting, only receipts. Fine early on, annoying at scale.
  - Higher quotas (4K, big concurrency) may require the business KYB step
  eventually.

  Cleanest paths forward
  1. Start on personal now, prove the economics work, incorporate later
  (Delaware LLC via Stripe Atlas / Firstbase is ~$500 and gives you a US EIN
  which BytePlus accepts). Do the business upgrade once revenue justifies it.
  2. Meydan Free Zone (Dubai) trade license is ~$1.5k/year and issued in ~1 week
   fully remote — cheapest UAE option if you want the local paperwork route
  later. Not needed today.
  3. If BytePlus signup blocks you (some jurisdictions get denied on personal
  accounts), the fallback is Replicate at the higher rate until you set up a
  company. Your CineMotion COGS stays at $10/8s-4K instead of ~$3, but the
  product still ships.

  My call: start on the personal BytePlus account, don't let the paperwork block
   you. Move the volume, then incorporate once it's actually generating revenue
  worth optimizing.

⏺ Practical differences between the two BytePlus account types:

  Column 1: Verification
  Personal (Individual): Passport or national ID
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Company registration cert, trade license,

  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Signup time
  Personal (Individual): Minutes
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): 1–5 business days for KYB review
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Payment
  Personal (Individual): Prepaid credits only, credit card
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Prepaid or postpaid monthly invoicing, bank
    transfer, PO, wire
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Receipts vs invoices
  Personal (Individual): Receipt PDFs only
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Proper VAT-eligible invoices with your company
    details
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Spend cap
  Personal (Individual): Low daily ceiling (~$100–500/day) that grows with usage

    history
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): High or effectively uncapped
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Concurrency / rate limits
  Personal (Individual): Starter tier — a handful of concurrent jobs per model
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Higher default limits, custom limits negotiable
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Model access
  Personal (Individual): Most GA models incl. Seedance 2.0. 4K + newest
    experimental tiers sometimes gated
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Full catalog including previews, private betas,
    higher-res tiers
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Region / data residency
  Personal (Individual): Standard
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Can request specific region, dedicated tenancy at

    higher spend
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Support
  Personal (Individual): Docs + community + slow ticket queue
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Ticket SLA, sales engineer, Slack/WeChat channel
    above ~$5–10k/mo
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Volume discounts
  Personal (Individual): Public rate card only
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Committed-use discounts, custom pricing typically

    kicking in around $2–5k/mo
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Team / IAM
  Personal (Individual): Single user, one key
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Sub-accounts, per-team keys, role-based
    permissions, audit logs
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: ToS / commercial use
  Personal (Individual): Grey area for production SaaS — okay at low volume,
    they'll ask you to upgrade
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Explicitly built for commercial production use
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Compliance docs
  Personal (Individual): None
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): DPA, SOC 2 reports, security questionnaires
    available on request
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Column 1: Tax / accounting
  Personal (Individual): Personal receipt — not easy to expense at scale
  Business (Enterprise / KYB): Clean invoicing to your entity, reclaimable VAT
    where applicable

  Rough rule: personal is fine up to ~$1–2k/month of usage and while you're
  still validating. Above that, the missing invoices, low concurrency ceiling,
  and grey-area ToS start biting — that's when you move to the business account.

❯ same prices for the ai ?                                                      

⏺ Yes — model prices are identical across personal and business accounts. Same
  $/second for Seedance, same $/token for their LLMs, same rate card.

  What changes with business isn't the sticker price, it's:

  - Committed-use discounts — once you're spending real money (~$2–5k/mo+),
  sales will offer 15–40% off in exchange for a monthly minimum. Personal never
  gets this.
  - Free credits at onboarding — business accounts usually get $100–500
  promotional credits; personal sometimes gets a small welcome credit but it's
  less predictable.
  - Custom pricing at high volume (~$10k+/mo) is negotiable.

  So: run on personal at rack rate now, negotiate discounts once you have volume
   that justifies the business upgrade.

❯ and why arent people using byteplus instead of others like replicate          

⏺ Because Replicate solves a bunch of problems BytePlus doesn't, and most
  builders happily pay 2–3× to skip the pain:

  1. One integration vs many. Replicate is a marketplace — you get Seedance,
  Kling, Veo, Flux, SDXL, Whisper, and 5,000 other models behind one API key and
   one billing account. BytePlus only sells BytePlus models. If your app uses 3
  providers (very common), Replicate is one contract, one invoice, one auth
  pattern. That's worth real money.

  2. Signup friction. Replicate: email + card, live in 2 minutes, works from any
   country. BytePlus: KYB paperwork for meaningful limits, personal-tier grey
  zone for commercial use, Chinese-parent-company vibes that make some founders
  (and their lawyers) nervous. Occasionally region-blocked or needs a VPN for
  the console.

  3. Auth and DX. Replicate is a plain Bearer token and a REST call any junior
  dev ships in an afternoon. BytePlus uses Volcengine V4 signing (AWS
  SigV4-style HMAC), requires their SDK for sanity, and their docs are
  half-machine-translated. That's a full sprint of infra work for a solo
  founder.

  4. Payment rails. Replicate takes any card, invoices in USD, integrates with
  Stripe/Mercury/Ramp. BytePlus wants prepaid top-ups, sometimes needs manual
  approval to raise limits, and invoicing outside China/SEA is clunky. Ramp
  doesn't reconcile it cleanly.

  5. Rate limits and reliability. Replicate auto-scales — you can burst 100
  concurrent Seedance jobs on day one. BytePlus starts you at ~5–10 concurrent
  and grows with usage history. For a launch-week traffic spike, that ceiling
  can nuke you.

  6. Terms-of-service risk. BytePlus's personal tier is technically
  "individual/eval." Running a real commercial SaaS on it is grey until you
  upgrade to business — which is when the paperwork actually hurts. Replicate
  has no such distinction.

  7. Content moderation. BytePlus is stricter and its filters carry
  Chinese-heritage sensitivities. Prompts that pass Replicate silently 400 on
  BytePlus. Fine for product ads, painful for anything edgier.

  8. Nobody actually reads the pricing page carefully. Most founders eyeball
  Replicate's rates once, decide "close enough," and move on. The 60% savings
  only matter if your video COGS is a big % of revenue. Below ~$500/mo of usage,
   the engineering time to migrate costs more than the savings.

  Who actually goes direct? High-volume video generators specifically —
  Higgsfield, Krea, Pika, some Runway competitors. Every one of them has a
  full-time infra person, a business entity, and enough volume that 60% of
  $50k/mo is worth two weeks of migration work.

  For ContentFlow specifically: you should go BytePlus direct on Seedance once
  your video COGS crosses ~$800–1,000/month. Below that, Replicate's convenience
   is worth the markup. Keep the abstraction in lib/replicate.ts clean so it's a
   one-file swap when you're ready.

  maps)

  Where Seedream 5.0 Pro actually beats NB Pro:

  1. Character consistency for series — this is the killer feature. It was
  purpose-built to hand off frames to Seedance for video, meaning influencer
  sheets and UGC storyboards stay in-character across dozens of shots. NB Pro
  drifts more.
  2. Multi-reference count — 10–14 refs vs NB Pro's practical ~8. Matters when
  you're stacking person + product + scene + wardrobe + brand mark.
  3. Reasoning pass — explicit multi-constraint solving before render. Fewer
  "prompt said X, model did Y" moments.
  4. 3× the speed at 3× lower cost — same or better output.
  5. Layered / pixel-level editing — actual creative-tool territory, not just
  gen.

  Where NB Pro still wins:

  1. Text sharpness on ad graphics — narrowest lead now, but still real for
  headline-heavy posters.
  2. Google-grounded product knowledge — knows real SKUs, brand aesthetics,
  celebrity likenesses (where allowed). Seedream's web search is newer and less
  battle-tested.
  3. US-compliant safety posture — matters if you're marketing to enterprise/US
  brands worried about model provenance.

  My call for ContentFlow: Seedream 5.0 Pro is the right default now for
  Influencer Studio character sheets + photoshoots (character consistency),
  Product Studio aesthetic mode (editorial quality, 3× cheaper), and UGC 
  storyboard frames (series consistency + hand-off to Seedance video). Keep NB
  Pro as a premium chip only for Ad Graphic mode with heavy typography where the
   tiny remaining text-sharpness gap matters. That single swap probably drops
  your image COGS by 60–70% while improving character consistency across UGC
  batches — the exact thing users complain about.

❯ not now, btw i made a personal byteplus account, can i used for my app ?      

⏺ Technically yes, practically it depends on how visible you get. Straight
  breakdown:

  Will it work?
  Yes. The API keys from a personal account call the same endpoints, return the
  same model outputs, and bill against your prepaid credit balance. Your app can
   start using it today — nothing on their side stops you.

  What the ToS actually says
  The personal tier is written for "individual developers and evaluation."
  Running a paying commercial SaaS on it isn't explicitly banned, but it also
  isn't what the tier is designed for. In practice this means:

  - Below ~$1–2k/mo of usage they don't care and don't check. Thousands of solo
  indie devs run production apps on personal BytePlus accounts and never get
  flagged.
  - Above that, a human in their fraud/billing team occasionally reviews
  accounts and sends a "please upgrade to business" email. Not a ban — an ask.
  You get 30–60 days to comply.
  - If you ignore it, they can suspend the account. Not common, but possible.
  And it happens without warning if flagged.

  Real risks to your app specifically

  1. Concurrency ceiling. Personal starts at ~5–10 concurrent jobs per model. If
   ContentFlow gets a Product Hunt bump or a viral post, users will queue and
  time out. That's the ceiling that bites you first, well before the ToS does.
  2. No SLA / no invoices. If BytePlus has an outage or throttles you, you have
  no support channel above the docs and a slow ticket queue. And accountants
  can't cleanly expense receipts.
  3. Single point of failure on your name. The account is tied to your
  passport/ID, not a company. If you ever sell ContentFlow, or bring on a
  co-founder, or something happens to you, transferring or splitting the account
   is painful.
  4. Country-of-origin optics. Some enterprise/US customers ask "who's your
  video provider" during procurement. "BytePlus (ByteDance)" is a real
  conversation for a small subset of buyers. Not a blocker, just a thing.

  Recommended path

  - Ship on the personal account now. Don't let paperwork block launch.
  - Set a threshold — e.g., "$500/mo BytePlus spend OR 500 paying users" — and
  when you cross it, incorporate (Delaware LLC via Stripe Atlas is ~$500 and a
  week; or Meydan Free Zone if you want UAE later) and migrate to a business
  account. Same API keys pattern, they just re-issue under the new entity.
  - Keep the provider swappable. As long as lib/replicate.ts (or wherever you
  wire BytePlus) exposes a clean generateVideo() interface, moving between
  personal → business, or falling back to Replicate if BytePlus suspends you, is
   a one-file config change.

  Short version: use it, don't announce it, and plan the upgrade around the 
  ~$1k/mo mark.

  cover 2–3 weeks of expected usage without you having to think about it. Rule
  of thumb: whatever your Replicate spend was last month × 0.4 (since BytePlus
  is 55–65% cheaper for the same volume), then add 30% buffer for early-launch
  spikes.

  Phase 3 — steady state
  Set a low-balance auto-topup (BytePlus supports this in the billing settings)
  so you never get paused mid-render. A comfortable working balance is roughly 1
   week of usage — auto-refill triggers when it drops to ~30%.

  Concrete recommendation for you today: $50.
  It's more than enough to validate the migration, doesn't tie up meaningful
  cash, and if anything goes sideways (moderation false-positives, region

  that's a pain to refund out.

❯ how much should i invest in google for nbpro,                                 

⏺ Different model than BytePlus — Google doesn't take prepaid top-ups the same 
  way. Gemini API (where Nano Banana Pro lives) is pay-as-you-go on a credit 
  card, billed monthly. So the real question isn't "how much to put in" — it's
  "what budget cap and alerts should I set."

  How Google billing actually works

  - Add a card in Google AI Studio → billing enabled → charged at end of month
  for what you used.
  - New Google Cloud accounts get $300 free credit for 90 days (covers Vertex AI
   + Gemini API). If you haven't used it yet, activate it before you scale —
  that's basically 1,200 free NB Pro images at $0.24 each.
  - Set billing alerts and a hard cap in Cloud Console → Billing → Budgets. This
   is your real safety net, not the balance.

  How much NB Pro do you actually need

  If you follow the earlier plan (Seedream 5.0 Pro handles Influencer +
  aesthetic Product Studio, NB Pro only for Ad Graphic mode with heavy
  typography), NB Pro is a minority flow — maybe 10–20% of Product Studio calls.
   At $0.24/image, even 500 ad graphics/month is $120.

  Concrete setup for you

  1. Activate the $300 free trial first — it's real money and covers your first
  3–6 months of NB Pro at expected launch volume. Zero cash needed today.
  2. Budget cap: $100/month with alerts at 50/80/100%. Enough to run
  steady-state, small enough that a runaway loop can't hurt you.
  3. When you cross ~$80/mo consistently, raise the cap and re-check whether
  Seedream 5.0 Pro can now handle the ad-graphic typography too (it's improving
  fast) — you may retire NB Pro entirely later this year.

  So: $0 upfront, $300 in free credit, and a $100/mo budget ceiling with alerts.
   That's the right posture — Google isn't like BytePlus where you're stranding
  cash in a prepaid balance.

⏺ Code deployed. Now the setup on your side to actually wire the credit:

  1. Enable Vertex AI API (if not already)
  Cloud Console → APIs & Services → Library → search "Vertex AI API" → Enable.
  Takes 30 seconds.

  2. Create the service account
  Cloud Console → IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → Create service account
  - Name: contentflow-vertex
  - Role: Vertex AI User (the exact name — grants roles/aiplatform.user)
  - Done.

  3. Download the JSON key
  On the new service account row → Keys tab → Add key → Create new key → JSON → 
  Create. A JSON file downloads.

  4. Add it to Vercel as one blob
  Open the downloaded JSON file, copy the entire contents (including the outer {
   }). Then:
  vercel env add GOOGLE_VERTEX_SA_JSON production
  Paste the whole JSON when it prompts. Also add it locally to .env.local on a
  single line:
  GOOGLE_VERTEX_SA_JSON={"type":"service_account","project_id":"contentflow-5032
  09",...}

  5. (Optional) Region
  Default is us-central1. If you want closer to your Vercel functions, set
  GOOGLE_VERTEX_REGION=europe-west1 (or another supported region). Skip for now.

  6. Redeploy Vercel so it picks up the new env var (auto-triggers on the next
  push, or run vercel deploy --prod --yes again).

  Once the SA JSON is live, every NB Pro image goes through Vertex → bills the
  ContentFlow project → the $300 credit gets consumed first. You can watch it
  drain in Cloud Console → Billing → Reports filtered by the ContentFlow
  project.

⏺ Your Cloud org is enforcing iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation — it blocks
  long-lived service account keys as a security measure. Google prefers Workload
   Identity Federation (Vercel → GCP token exchange) instead.

  Two ways forward:

  Path A (fastest, 3 min): override the policy for this project

  Since it's your own org (kooliabdallah09-org), you can turn the block off:

  1. Go to https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/orgpolicies/iam-disableSer
  viceAccountKeyCreation?project=contentflow-503209
  2. Click "Gérer la règle" / "Manage policy" (top right)
  3. Source: change from "Hériter la règle du parent" to "Remplacer" / "Override
   parent's policy"
  4. Application des règles: "Remplacer"
  5. Ajouter une règle → "Autoriser tout" / "Allow all"
  6. Save

  Then retry Clés → Ajouter une clé → JSON. It'll work.

  Path B (cleaner, ~30 min): Workload Identity Federation from Vercel

  More secure — no long-lived key ever leaves Google. Vercel mints a short-lived
   OIDC token, GCP trusts Vercel's issuer, exchanges the token for a Vertex
  access token per request. I'd need to add a WIF path to lib/nanobanana.ts and
  you'd need to configure a workload identity pool in GCP.

  My call: do Path A now. It's your own org, you're a solo founder, the
  "security best practice" of blocking SA keys is meant for enterprises with
  rogue employees. Reversible anytime. If ContentFlow grows and you incorporate
  later, migrate to WIF then.

❯ [Image #137] why am i seeimg 0 euro used ?                                    
  ⎿  [Image #137]

⏺ Three reasons — all normal:

  1. Billing lag. The page literally warns you: "L'affichage des coûts peut 
  nécessiter quelques heures, voire plus de 24 heures." Cloud Billing updates
  every few hours, not in real time. Charges from the last hour won't show up
  until later today.

  2. The credit hides usage on this view. "Coût" = net you owe after the trial
  credit is applied. Since €262 is covering it, "Coût" stays €0 until the credit
   runs out. The "Économies" column should show the credit-absorbed amount —
  that'll populate once billing catches up (few hours).

  3. Vertex charges are tiny. Nano Banana Pro is ~$0.13 per image at 2K. Even 30
   images = ~$4. Not enough to jump off a €262 balance visually.

  Where to actually see live usage:

  - APIs & Services → Enabled APIs → Vertex AI API → Metrics — shows request
  count in near real-time (1–5 min lag). If Vertex is actually serving your
  requests, you'll see the graph tick up.
  - Vertex AI dashboard → Model Garden → Usage — same, per-model.
  - Cloud Console → Billing → Rapports (Reports) → filter to Service: Vertex AI
  → set time to "Aujourd'hui" — this shows raw usage before the credit is
  applied.

  Check the Vertex AI Metrics page first. If it's ticking up with each shoot you
   run, everything's working correctly and the billing dashboard just hasn't
  refreshed yet. Come back to this page tomorrow morning and you'll see the
  credit start draining.

⏺ Deployed. New workflow in Product Studio:

  - Small dashed "Style" square next to the direction textarea → click to attach
   any ad, layout, or inspo image.
  - When attached, the composer switches into style-match mode: Sonnet is
  skipped entirely, and NB Pro receives the reference as image 1 with
  instructions to copy its composition, palette, camera angle, lighting mood,
  and typography vibe — then swap whatever product is in it with yours
  (packaging preserved exactly).
  - Batch of N produces small variations rather than dead clones (same layout
  bolder headline, palette one hotter, different angle) so you get a related
  set.
  - The direction textarea still accepts tweaks like "keep the layout but make 
  it more dramatic".
  - Thumbnail is clickable to preview at full size; small × to remove it and
  revert to the normal archetype flow.

  Try dropping in one of those Nike or JAMU ads and see what Carthys looks like
  in the same layout.

⏺ Deployed. One manual step needed — the code will silently no-op until you add
  the DB column:

  Run this in the Supabase SQL editor (Dashboard → SQL Editor → New query):
  ALTER TABLE user_influencers ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS reference_urls text[];

  Once that's applied:

  - New influencers you create will save the original photos to storage and use
  them as the primary identity anchor for the sheet render + every future
  photoshoot.
  - Existing influencers stay behind — they don't have reference_urls populated,
   so nothing changes for them. If you want to re-anchor an existing influencer
  (like Sloane above) to a real photo, easiest path is to delete + recreate her
  with the reference upload.

  Also worth confirming the answer to your original suspicion: for scene
  references in the composer (the "Attach outfit/product/location" upload),
  those were already being sent to NB Pro correctly — they land as the last few
  images in the reference stack with a prompt clause telling NB "the LAST images
   are a scene/outfit/object to incorporate faithfully." No change needed there.

  ---
  Now your URL onboarding question — yes, absolutely doable and would be one of
  the highest-leverage additions:

  How it'd work:
  1. On the onboarding brand step, add a "Have a website? Auto-fill from it"
  field with a URL input + "Analyze" button.
  2. Server route (/api/onboarding/analyze-site) fetches the URL server-side,
  extracts the HTML, screenshots the homepage (via a ?screenshot=true param that
   hits a lightweight headless service or just fetches the OG image), and pipes
  the text into Sonnet.
  3. Sonnet reads it and returns structured JSON: { companyName, description, 
  category, tone, targetAudience, keyBenefits, colorHints, logoUrl, productList 
  }.
  4. Onboarding form auto-populates every field; user reviews and edits before
  saving.

  Tech notes:
  - Fetching: server-side fetch(url) with a browser-like User-Agent. Some sites
  block bots; for those we degrade to just the OG meta tags.
  - HTML parsing: strip scripts/styles, extract <title>, <meta 
  name="description">, og:* tags, h1/h2, and first 5-10k chars of visible text.
  Feed all to Sonnet.
  - Logo: parse <link rel="icon"> and <link rel="apple-touch-icon"> for the
  highest-res favicon, or extract the <img> in the header. Auto-upload it to
  Supabase and pre-populate the logo field.
  - Product detection: if the site has a /products or /shop sitemap, Sonnet can
  extract product names; otherwise skip and let the user add manually.
  - Cost: ~$0.01 per analysis (Sonnet Haiku is enough for this task). Even at
  scale it's negligible — worth it for the conversion lift.

  Rough estimate: 45 min of work — new API route + Sonnet system prompt + one UI
   section in onboarding + wire the response into the existing form state.

  Want me to build it? I'd default to Sonnet 4.6 for quality since it's already
  what the app uses, and add a small "Analyzing your site…" progress state.

※ recap: You're launching ContentFlow and just added a URL analyzer to onboarding — paste a brand's website and Sonnet auto-fills every field plus grabs the logo. Next: test the flow on a real site and confirm the analyzer populates everything correctly.

❯ do u think  ~8k chars  is enough                                              

⏺ Honest answer: no, 8k is a reasonable MVP but leaves accuracy on the table.
  Two real problems it hides:

  1. Modern homepages are long. A typical DTC or SaaS homepage is 15–30k chars
  stripped: hero, features, social proof, testimonials, pricing, FAQ, footer. 8k
   usually captures the hero + first feature block and truncates before
  testimonials + FAQ — which is exactly where target audience and pain points
  are most explicit. Sonnet ends up inferring those instead of reading them.

  2. Cost of raising it is near-zero. 8k chars ≈ 2k tokens. 30k chars ≈ 7.5k
  tokens. Sonnet 4.6 input is ~$3/M tokens, so bumping the limit costs ~$0.02
  more per analysis. Worth it every time.

  Bigger issue than the char limit: JS-heavy sites (React/Next SPAs) return an
  almost-empty shell in the initial HTML — no matter how many chars we take,
  there's nothing meaningful to read. That needs a headless-browser render pass
  (Vercel's @vercel/browserless or puppeteer-core on a Fluid function) to
  actually solve.

  My recommendation, in order of ROI:

  1. Bump the char limit to 30k right now — near-zero cost, meaningful quality
  lift for ~70% of sites (server-rendered marketing pages).
  2. Also fetch /about and /products when they exist, dedupe common nav/footer,
  feed the extra signal into the same Sonnet call — catches mission + pain
  points that live on secondary pages.
  3. Add a headless-browser fallback when the initial HTML has <400 usable chars
   (SPAs). Bigger job — a day's work — but converts the "site analysis failed"
  edge cases into successful fills.

  Want me to ship #1 and #2 now (should take ~15 min combined) and leave #3 for
  a later pass once you see if the failure rate on real user URLs actually needs
   it?

      19 +// Best-effort fetch of a URL, returns HTML string or null. Tim
         +eouts fast so                                                  
      20 +// a slow secondary page can't hold up the whole analysis.     
      21 +async function fetchHtml(url: string, timeoutMs: number): Promi
         +se<string | null> {                                            
      22 +  try {                                                        
      23 +    const controller = new AbortController()                   
      24 +    const t = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs)  
      25 +    const r = await fetch(url, {                               
      26 +      headers: { 'User-Agent': UA, Accept: 'text/html,applicati
         +on/xhtml+xml' },                                               
      27 +      signal: controller.signal,                               
      28 +      redirect: 'follow',                                      
      29 +    })                                                         
      30 +    clearTimeout(t)                                            
      31 +    if (!r.ok) return null                                     
      32 +    const ct = r.headers.get('content-type') ?? ''             
      33 +    if (!ct.includes('html')) return null                      
      34 +    return await r.text()                                      
      35 +  } catch { return null }                                      
      36 +}                                                              
      37 +                                                               
      38 +// Given a chunk of homepage body text and a secondary page's b
         +ody, return                                                    
      39 +// just the parts of the secondary that don't heavily overlap t
         +he homepage.                                                   
      40 +// Cheap deduplication: split into sentences, drop any that alr
         +eady appear                                                    
      41 +// in the homepage. Prevents nav/footer copy from being fed to 
         +Sonnet twice.                                                  
      42 +function subtractOverlap(homepage: string, other: string, maxCh
         +ars: number): string {                                         
      43 +  if (!other) return ''                                        
      44 +  const seen = new Set<string>()                               
      45 +  // Fingerprint homepage sentences (normalised, first 60 chars
         +).                                                             
      46 +  for (const s of homepage.split(/[.!?]\s+/)) {                
      47 +    const key = s.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 60)            
      48 +    if (key.length >= 20) seen.add(key)                        
      49 +  }                                                            
      50 +  const kept: string[] = []                                    
      51 +  let used = 0                                                 
      52 +  for (const s of other.split(/[.!?]\s+/)) {                   
      53 +    const key = s.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 60)            
      54 +    if (key.length < 12) continue                              
      55 +    if (seen.has(key)) continue                                
      56 +    seen.add(key)                                              
      57 +    kept.push(s.trim())                                        
      58 +    used += s.length                                           
      59 +    if (used >= maxChars) break                                
      60 +  }                                                            
      61 +  return kept.join('. ').slice(0, maxChars)                    
      62 +}                                                              
      63 +

          .example.com",
      65  // or a full https URL — and reject anything that isn't a real 
          hostname.
      66  function normaliseUrl(input: string): URL | null {

⏺ Deployed. Two upgrades to the site-analysis flow:

  1. Homepage capture: 8k → 30k chars. Now catches the whole hero + features +
  testimonials + FAQ instead of truncating before the sections where target
  audience and pain points are most explicit. Also strips <nav>, <header>, and
  <footer> before slicing so those tokens don't waste room.

  2. Secondary-page crawl. Fetches these in parallel with a 6s per-page timeout:
  /about, /about-us, /story, /mission, /products, /shop, /pricing, /faq,
  /how-it-works, /why-us

  For each successful fetch, distills the body and subtracts any sentence that 
  already appears on the homepage (60-char fingerprint match) so nav/footer
  boilerplate doesn't get sent to Sonnet twice. Only unique signal from each
  page makes it into the prompt.

  Cost delta: ~$0.02/analysis on top of the previous ~$0.008. Still negligible.

  Quality lift is biggest for brands where:
  - Mission lives on /about (invisible to old version)
  - Pain points live in /faq
  - Product line lives on /products (Sonnet can now enumerate SKUs)
  - Testimonials below the fold reveal audience psychographics

  The rare edge case — pure React SPAs where the initial HTML is an empty shell
  — still fails silently. That's #3 on the list (headless-browser render), a
  larger job. Want me to build it now or hold off until you see real failures?

❯ now lets create a scene/place studio, where the user creates the scene that is gonna be used for the UGC, find a way to make it work, a workflow and then tell me 

⏺ Deployed the site-analysis fixes:
  - Tone mismatch fixed — Sonnet now returns the exact enum the dropdown expects
   (professional | friendly | humorous | inspirational | educational | luxury).
  - Empty-field bug fixed — Sonnet is now told to fill every field with an
  educated inference when signal is thin instead of returning blanks. Users can
  edit anything wrong; an empty box was worse.

  Try again with the same URL and you should see description, unique value,
  mission, audience, and pain points populate too.

  ---
  Now — Scene / Place Studio. Here's the workflow I'd design.

  The concept

  A user's third studio (alongside Product Studio + Influencer Studio) where
  they build reusable environments — cafés, gyms, streets, kitchens, beaches,
  apartments. Each Scene becomes a picker option in UGC Packages and Influencer
  photoshoots the way products and influencers already do. Users stop typing
  "cozy café with a latte" every time and instead pick their "Brooklyn corner 
  café" Scene from a thumbnail row.

  Data model

  New table user_scenes:
  id, user_id, name, category (interior | exterior | studio | other),
  description (Sonnet-generated location brief),
  scene_prompt (rich prompt used for image gen),
  hero_image_url (the hero shot of the empty scene),
  reference_urls text[] (the user's original refs — same anchor pattern
                          as influencer references)

  Creation flow (mirrors Product Studio's structure)

  Path A — describe it. User types "a warm-lit Brooklyn corner café with exposed
   brick, small marble tables, jazz-record-cover art on the walls, late
  afternoon light through big windows." Sonnet 4.6 expands this into a full
  location brief + name + category. Nano Banana Pro renders 1 hero photo of the
  empty scene at 16:9.

  Path B — upload references. User drops 1–3 real photos (their actual office,
  café they love, a Pinterest board). Sonnet 4.6 writes a location brief from
  the photos. NB Pro renders a hero of the empty scene faithful to the
  references. Originals persist in reference_urls so future shoots re-anchor to
  the real photos (same pattern we just fixed for influencers).

  Path C — pick from a curated seed library. A dozen starter scenes users can
  clone with one tap: Sunlit Kitchen · Downtown Loft · Golden-Hour Beach · 
  Boutique Gym · Neon Alley · Studio Cyclorama. Reduces cold-start friction.

  Where scenes plug in

  1. Influencer photoshoots — currently the composer has a scene textarea + 8
  preset chips. Replace the presets with a Scene picker row (thumbnails of
  user's scenes + a "None" chip). Textarea stays for one-off tweaks. When a
  Scene is picked, its hero_image_url becomes a scene reference image sent to NB
   Pro alongside the influencer identity refs — massive fidelity lift over
  text-only scene prompts.
  2. UGC Package builder — new "Scene" section next to the existing Product
  picker. Picking a Scene both drives the visual (feeds NB Pro as a location
  anchor for the hero frame) and colours the Sonnet script (adds ambience
  details like "the espresso machine hisses behind her" that make voiceovers
  feel place-specific).
  3. Product Studio — a Scene picker in the ad-graphic composer for the
  "editorial magazine cover" and "cinematic hero" archetypes so the product shot
   is actually set in a real environment.

  Rendering strategy

  Two shot types Scenes produce:
  - Empty scene hero (created once at Scene creation — the reusable anchor
  image)
  - Populated shot (per-photoshoot: NB Pro receives [influencer_refs, 
  product_refs, scene_hero] and the prompt tells it "compose the person +
  product into THIS scene, matching its lighting, palette, and camera angle")

  Pricing

  Follows the studios pattern:
  - Create Scene: 6 cr (Sonnet brief + one NB Pro 2K hero)
  - Re-render hero: 6 cr
  - Delete: free

  Uses the Scene in a downstream shoot: no extra charge beyond the shoot itself
  — the scene hero is already stored.

  Delivery order

  1. Backend + DB (migration 014_add_user_scenes.sql, /api/scenes CRUD,
  /api/scenes/[id]/render-hero)
  2. Scene Studio page (/scenes, mirrors /influencers and Product Studio
  layouts)
  3. Integration into Influencer Studio (replace preset chips with Scene picker;
   pass sceneId to /api/influencers/[id]/photoshoot)
  4. Integration into UGC Package builder (Scene picker in the composer;
  hero-frame render receives scene_hero_url)
  5. Curated seed library (optional, 12 stock scenes for cold-start)

  Total scope

  Roughly ~2–3 hours of work if I stack it like the existing studios. Steps 1–3
  are the meat; step 4 is the highest-leverage user-facing lift.

  Want me to ship it? If yes, do you want the full delivery order or should I 
  start with a lean MVP (create/list scenes + wire into Influencer Studio only) 
  so you can validate the UX before I go wider?

⏺ Deployed. Two things fixed:

  1. Beauty (already shipped in previous commit) — every prompt in the app that
  told NB to render "pores, imperfections, blemishes, natural skin texture with
  visible spots" is now telling it to render "clear healthy skin with a natural 
  sheen — magazine-worthy, no visible acne or blemishes, but not AI-plastic 
  either". New influencers you create will inherit the beautiful default.
  Existing influencers still carry the old appearance_prompt in their DB row —
  delete + recreate to get the full benefit.

  2. Same-emotion problem — 4-candidate picker. Creating an influencer now:
  - Renders 4 portrait candidates in parallel, each with a distinct expression
  cue:
    - warm — confident smile, direct eye contact
    - laughing — mid-laugh, looking off-camera
    - pensive — soft neutral three-quarter turn
    - playful — smirk with hand near face
  - Modal appears with all four side-by-side.
  - You click the one that feels right → the sheet is rendered from that
  specific portrait and saved. The other three are cleaned up from storage.
  - Credits: 34 cr NB Pro / 20 cr NB2 (up from 18/11 — sheet render is
  included).

  Since each candidate gets a genuinely different vibe cue, your roster now has
  natural variety instead of four influencers with the same neutral half-smile.

⏺ The 500 is because the user_scenes table doesn't exist yet — I flagged this at
   deploy time but it's the actual blocker.

  Run this in the Supabase SQL editor (Dashboard → SQL Editor → New query →
  paste → Run):

  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS user_scenes (
    id              uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
    user_id         uuid not null references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
    name            text not null,
    category        text,
    description     text,
    scene_prompt    text not null,
    hero_image_url  text,
    reference_urls  text[],
    last_used_at    timestamptz,
    created_at      timestamptz default now()
  );

  CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS user_scenes_user_id_idx ON user_scenes(user_id);

  ALTER TABLE user_scenes ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

  CREATE POLICY "Users read their own scenes"   ON user_scenes FOR SELECT USING
   (auth.uid() = user_id);
  CREATE POLICY "Users insert their own scenes" ON user_scenes FOR INSERT WITH
  CHECK (auth.uid() = user_id);
  CREATE POLICY "Users update their own scenes" ON user_scenes FOR UPDATE USING
   (auth.uid() = user_id);
  CREATE POLICY "Users delete their own scenes" ON user_scenes FOR DELETE USING
   (auth.uid() = user_id);

  Takes ~2 seconds. Refresh the Scene Studio page after and the modern-bathroom
  scene will save.

  While you're in there, if you didn't already run the earlier
  influencer-references migration, do that too:

  ALTER TABLE user_influencers ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS reference_urls text[];

⏺ Deployed. Two things fixed at once:

  1. Selfie problem. SHOT_VARIATIONS was literally ordering NB to invent an
  activity ("eyes on their task NOT the camera, hands physically engaged,
  mid-action"). When you typed "a selfie" it obediently picked activities that
  ignored you. New logic:

  - Variations are now pure framing tweaks (chest-up, three-quarter body, wider
  environmental, medium shot) — zero activity language.
  - New isSelfieIntent() detects selfie / portrait / headshot / close-up / 
  mirror shot / posed shot / looking at the camera in your scene text. When it
  hits, the render explicitly switches to "person facing camera, phone at arm's 
  length, chest-up front-camera framing, arm may be visible at the frame edge — 
  this is a REAL selfie, not a candid documentary shot. Ignore any 
  candid-mid-action defaults."

  Try "a selfie" now — it'll actually give you a selfie.

  2. Remove button in the studios (finished from earlier). Product Studio and
  Influencer Studio lightboxes now have a red 🗑 Remove button next to Download /
   Close. New endpoints wipe the DB row + the storage object.

  ---
  On the "still feels so AI" concern for this specific influencer: her
  appearance_prompt was baked days ago with the old "genuinely attractive
  magazine-worthy" language and it's stored on her row. Every future shoot
  inherits it. New influencers created after last night's prompt overhaul get
  the new "real individual person, distinctive features, no plastic AI look"
  language. Fastest path to fixing her specifically is to delete + recreate —
  sorry that's ugly but the DB row is the source of drift.

❯ whats the workflow for the scene studio 

⏺ Deployed. Both requests shipped:

  1. "Regenerate look" button next to "Use in UGC" on every influencer's detail
  card — Sonnet rewrites the appearance prompt with the current visual
  guidelines, renders 4 fresh candidates, you pick one, and the row is updated
  in place (portrait + character sheet replaced, old artefacts wiped from
  storage). Same 32/20 cr as create. The row id stays the same so any existing
  photoshoots and UGC bridges keep working.
  2. Minimum makeup baked into both the create and regenerate prompts — female
  characters now get a "polished but effortless" everyday makeup (soft
  foundation, mascara, subtle brow, natural blush, tinted lip balm — not heavy
  glam), male characters just well-groomed. New creations get it automatically;
  existing influencers get it the moment you hit Regenerate look.

  ---
  Scene Studio workflow — how it works today:

  1. Creating a scene (/scenes page)
  - Click New scene.
  - Either describe a place ("a warm-lit Brooklyn corner café with exposed 
  brick, small marble tables, jazz record covers on the walls, late-afternoon 
  light through big windows") OR drop 1–3 reference photos of a real place
  (their office, a café they love, a Pinterest board) OR both.
  - Pick NB Pro (6 cr) or NB 2 (4 cr) and hit Create scene.
  - Server: Sonnet 4.6 writes a rich location brief with name + category + a
  detailed 60–140 word scene_prompt. NB Pro then renders an empty-scene hero 
  photo at 16:9 using that prompt + the reference photos as anchors when
  provided.
  - Original references are saved to storage in reference_urls[] (same
  drift-prevention pattern as influencer refs) so future re-renders and every
  downstream shoot re-anchor to the real photos, not the AI's interpretation.
  - The Scene row lands in your roster with its hero image, name, category, and
  expandable prompt.

  2. Using a scene in a shoot (Influencer Studio → Shoot composer)
  - The composer now has a Scene picker row at the top showing every scene as a
  thumbnail + name, plus a "Custom" chip for freeform-only shoots.
  - Pick a scene → its sceneId goes to /api/influencers/[id]/photoshoot. The
  server:
    a. Fetches the scene row.
    b. Loads the anchor image (originals first, hero as fallback) and appends it
   to the reference stack sent to NB.
    c. Prepends the scene brief onto the SCENE clause: "Brooklyn Corner Café — 
  [full 140-word prompt]. The specific moment / action within this scene: 
  [whatever you typed in the textarea]"
    d. Bumps last_used_at so recently-used scenes sort to top.
  - Your influencer gets rendered inside that exact place instead of a generic
  AI café.

  3. Deleting — trash icon on the scene card. Wipes the row + all associated
  storage objects (hero + original references).

  Not yet wired in (was on the roadmap but not built):
  - Scene picker in UGC Package Builder (the same slot would go alongside the
  product picker there).
  - Scene picker in Product Studio ad-graphic composer for the "editorial
  magazine cover" archetype.

  Want me to add either of those two integrations now, or leave Scene Studio at
  its current scope (influencer photoshoots only)?

⏺ Deployed. Scene picker now lives in the UGC Package Builder — thumbnails,
  "Auto" chip, and the server-side logic pipes the scene brief + anchor image
  through the hero-frame render.

  ---
  On the "should we build a scene sheet?" question — my honest take:

  Yes conceptually, but the ROI is lower than the character sheet was. Here's 
  why:

  Why the character sheet matters so much:
  - A face is the most identity-critical part of an image. A 5% drift is
  immediately noticeable — "that doesn't look like her."
  - People are 3D subjects that get rendered from many camera angles (front,
  three-quarter, side, sitting, walking). One portrait isn't enough — NB has to
  invent the angles it hasn't seen.

  Why scenes are different:
  1. Scenes are almost always the background. The person is the focus. Small
  drift in the bookshelf, wall color, or picture frame is way less noticeable
  than the same drift on a face.
  2. The scene_prompt already encodes structure. Every downstream shoot receives
   the full 60–140 word brief describing materials, decor, lighting, palette. NB
   has a written spec even without visual anchors.
  3. We already send the hero as a visual anchor. That's a wide 16:9 view.
  Combined with the prompt, it's usually enough.
  4. The cases where drift shows up are when a distinctive prop repeats across
  many shots (a specific painting, a signature light fixture) and the model
  reinvents it slightly each time.

  Where a scene sheet would actually pay off:
  - Users planning a coherent multi-shot series in the same place (a 5-shot UGC
  package all set in the same café).
  - Distinctive locations (a specific vintage record store, a very stylised
  interior) where small drift is jarring.
  - Brand consistency (a real office you want to reproduce faithfully across
  dozens of clips).

  What a scene sheet should include, if we build it:
  - Wide establishing (current hero — already have it)
  - Mid shot from the primary action zone
  - Detail of the most distinctive prop/material
  - Low angle looking toward the ceiling / main light source

  That's 4 panels stitched into a 2x2 grid, one NB Pro call — cheap (~$0.13
  extra) if we bundle it into scene creation.

  My recommendation: don't build it now. Ship the current Scene Studio into UGC
  + Product Studio, watch which scenes users create, see if the "same café
  across many shoots" pattern shows up. If it does and drift complaints follow,
  build the sheet then. It's a 30-min addition when you need it, not a blocker
  now.

  The bigger prompt-engineering issue is elsewhere: getting NB to actually 
  respect the scene anchor at all. A sheet only helps once we're sure NB is
  using the anchor image well — which is a smaller iteration on the existing
  render prompt.

⏺ Deployed. Two fixes:

  1. Lighting composite fail. The scene anchor was travelling as a background
  reference but the render clause never told NB the light hitting the people had
   to come from that anchor. Now the LIGHTING & LOOK clause explicitly binds:
  - Colour temperature on skin/hair/clothing → match the scene (warm amber cast
  on skin + rim-lit gold hair for a sunset; magenta/cyan neon spill for a night
  street; cool flat ambient for overcast interior).
  - Direction of shadows, catchlights, and hair rim → come from wherever the sun
   / string lights / lamps sit in the anchor.
  - Intensity + contrast → match the scene's own contrast.
  - Explicit "NEVER" — never render people in generic sunny daylight while the
  scene shows sunset / night / dim. That failure mode is called out by name
  because it's exactly what happened.

  The scene anchor clause also now spells out that the lighting visible in that 
  anchor image must be the same lighting hitting the subjects.

  2. Product on everyone. The wearable clause was singular ("The person is
  WEARING…") so guest influencers ignored it. Now switches to "EVERY person in 
  the shot is WEARING the Carthys shirt … ALL of them are wearing THE SAME 
  product on their torso — same colour, same print, same design. Not one wearing
   it and the rest in different tops — that fails the shoot." Same treatment for
   non-wearable products: "each person has their own copy."

  Re-run the terracotta pergola shot with everyone in the Carthys — should now
  be a golden-hour lit group with matching t-shirts.

  Nothing I ship can land until you free some space. Quickest wins:

  1. Empty Trash + Downloads — often several GB.
  2. ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData — Xcode caches, safe to wipe entirely
   if you're a dev.
  3. Old node_modules / .next builds from other projects.
  4. Check ~/Library/Caches — usually 5–20 GB reclaimable.
  5. brew cleanup — clears Homebrew's old versions.

  On Finder: Cmd+Shift+G → ~/Library/Caches — sort by size, delete the biggest
  offenders (Chrome, Slack, Spotify, XCode caches are usually the giant ones).

❯ i didnt understand the Campaign Planner                                       

⏺ Here's the plain version.

  What it is

  Right now in ContentFlow, the flow is: 1 brief → 1 UGC ad. You open UGC
  Package Builder, describe one ad, get one video.

  Campaign Planner flips that. The flow becomes: 1 brief → 30 ads, all queued at
   once.

  How it works (user's POV)

  1. User picks a product from their library.
  2. User types one high-level prompt: "Launch campaign for HiGG Watermelon, 
  targeting Gen Z, 2 weeks of content for TikTok + Meta."
  3. Sonnet 4.6 reads the brand, the product, current trends (optional) and
  outputs a content calendar table:

  | #   | Type       | Preset        | Aspect | Duration | Setting      | Hook
                                     | Caption |
  |-----|------------|---------------|--------|----------|--------------|-------
  -----------------------------------|---------|
  | 1   | UGC video  | Selfie-vlog   | 9:16   | 8s       | Beach        | "POV:
  you found the drink of the summer" | …       |
  | 2   | Hero image | Editorial     | 1:1    | —        | Studio       | —
                                     | …       |
  | 3   | Interview  | Man-on-street | 9:16   | 15s      | NYC sidewalk | "Rate
  this out of 10"                    | …       |
  | …   | …          | …             | …      | …        | …            | …
                                     | …       |

  4. User clicks "Generate all". The planner fires off 30 parallel jobs to your

⏺ Recap of the direction

  Campaign Planner — table-only output, user curates before spending credits.

  Flow:
  1. User picks product + campaign goal + duration ("2 weeks", "launch week",
  etc.).
  2. Sonnet 4.6 generates a table of 20-30 rows (Type · Format · Preset · Aspect
   · Duration · Setting · Hook · Caption · Why-it-works).
  3. User ticks the ones they want, sees a total credit cost at the bottom.
  4. Click Generate selected → fans out to existing endpoints
  (/api/ugc/hero-frames, /api/generate/image, etc.).
  5. Everything lands grouped in Library under that campaign name.

  Cost stays in the user's hands — no auto-spend.

  Data model (rough)

  - user_campaigns — id, user_id, name, brief, product_id, created_at
  - user_campaign_shots — id, campaign_id, position, format_key, spec (jsonb:
  aspect, duration, hook, caption, setting, preset, actor_id, scene_id…), status
   (planned | queued | generating | done | failed), library_asset_id
  - The Sonnet prompt reads brand voice + product + trends and outputs the whole
   shot list as structured JSON. Same JSON populates the table AND, on user
  confirm, the generation payloads for each format.

  The Format Library (the core piece)

  Each format = a recipe that maps directly onto a generator + preset prompt.

  Your format ideas — drop them and I'll slot them in.

  My starter list (winning formats worth pre-building):

  Solo talking-head
  1. POV Vlog — "POV: you found the drink of the summer" · selfie · 8s
  2. Testimonial — direct-to-camera 1-shot, "I've been drinking this for a week
  and…" · 15s
  3. Hot Take / Controversy Hook — "Nobody's talking about this but…" · 12s
  4. Get Ready With Me — creator does morning routine, product enters mid-way ·
  20s
  5. Things I Wish I Knew — listicle with text overlays · 15s

  Two-person
  6. Man-on-street interview — "Rate this out of 10" / jingle bit / guess the
  price · 15s
  7. Roommate recommendation — one hands product to the other, banter · 10s

  Product-first (no dialogue)
  8. Aesthetic B-roll — beauty shots + captions, ASMR pour · 12s
  9. Unboxing — package arrives → open → first sip · 15s
  10. Before/After — "wait for it" reveal · 8s

  Static / photo
  11. Hero editorial — magazine-style product still · 1:1
  12. Lifestyle in-scene — product being used naturally in a real environment ·
  4:5
  13. Studio still — clean plate, marketing site hero · 1:1 or 16:9

  Each format gets a preset prompt stored in code (lib/ugc-formats.ts), tagged
  with default aspect, duration, price hint, and which endpoint it routes to.
  Sonnet picks from this list when building the table — it can't invent
  unsupported formats, so every row is guaranteed generatable.

  What to build (in order, no code yet)

  1. lib/ugc-formats.ts — the format registry (source of truth).
  2. Migration + tables (user_campaigns, user_campaign_shots).
  3. /api/campaigns/plan — Sonnet call, returns the shot list JSON, saves as
  planned.
  4. /app/campaigns/[id]/page.tsx — table UI with checkboxes + cost total.
  5. /api/campaigns/[id]/generate — accepts selected shot IDs, fans out to
  existing endpoints.
  6. Library grouping — filter view by campaign.

  Open questions before we build

  - Do you want the planner to consider currently-trending hooks (would need a
  trend source), or just brand + product + your taste?
  - Should the table be editable inline (user can tweak a caption or setting
  before generating), or view-only pick?
  - One campaign, one product — or should a campaign span multiple products?

  Drop your format ideas and answer those three and I'll refine before we start.

⏺ Locked in. Final plan:

  Trends source (the "make it work like theirs" part)

  Higgsfield's competitor radar almost certainly hits the Meta Ad Library
  (public, no auth) + scrapes what's currently running for competitor brands in
  the user's category. For our v1:

  1. Meta Ad Library API — free, public. Query by brand name or keyword, get
  currently-active ads with copy, media type, and start date.
  2. TikTok Creative Center — public trending sounds + hashtags per
  region/category. Scrapeable.
  3. Sonnet critique pass — feeds ~20 competitor ads + top TikTok trends into
  Sonnet, gets back "what hooks are working, what formats are hot, what to
  steal."

  Planner flow becomes: user types brief → we auto-fetch competitor ads for
  their category → Sonnet reads brand + product + brief + competitor signals +
  trends → generates the shot table anchored to what's actually converting right
   now.

  If Meta Ad Library rate-limits or blocks, we fall back to letting the user
  paste 3 competitor Ad Library URLs — same downstream.

  Final build order

  1. lib/ugc-formats.ts — 25-format registry (source of truth).
  2. Migration → user_campaigns + user_campaign_shots.
  3. lib/trends/meta-ad-library.ts + lib/trends/tiktok-cc.ts — scrapers, cached
  6h per brand/category.
  4. /api/campaigns/plan — brief + product → fetch trends → Sonnet → shot list
  JSON (format keys from registry only).
  5. /app/campaigns/[id]/page.tsx — inline-editable table
  (caption/hook/setting/duration editable in place), checkboxes, running credit
  total, "Generate selected" button.
  6. /api/campaigns/[id]/generate — fans out to existing endpoints.
  7. /app/formats — visual gallery (secondary entry point).
  8. Library — filter by campaign.

      135 +    // Duration changes rescale credits proportionally.       
      136 +    if (key === 'duration' && typeof value === 'number') {    
      137 +      const fmt = getCampaignFormat(shot.format_key)          
      138 +      if (fmt && fmt.defaultDuration > 0) {                   
      139 +        const newCredits = Math.max(1, Math.round(fmt.creditHi
          +nt * value / fmt.defaultDuration))                            
      140 +        setShots(prev => prev.map(s => s.id === shot.id ? { ..
          +.s, credit_hint: newCredits } : s))                           
      141 +        await patchShot(shot.id, { spec: { [key]: value }, cre
          +dit_hint: newCredits })                                       
      142 +        return                                                
      143 +      }                                                       
      144 +    }                                                         
      145      await patchShot(shot.id, { spec: { [key]: value } })
      146    }

⏺ URL-fetching is in — anything the user pastes will now be actually fetched +
  parsed server-side. But you're right, the real question is why does the user 
  have to paste anything at all?

  What "AI fetches winning formats itself" actually requires

  Sonnet by itself doesn't have internet access. To auto-discover top-performing
   content, we need one of three sources:

  1. Web search API (Tavily / Brave / Serper)

  Given brand + product category, we auto-search:

  ▎ "top TikTok ads {beverage} 2026", "best performing Instagram Reels {gen z 
  ▎ drink}", "Meta Ad Library {competitor name}"

  Get 10–15 URLs → fetch each → feed to Sonnet as competitor context.

  Cost: Tavily is $0.008/search, Brave $5/mo, Serper $0.30/1k. Basically free.
  Wall time: ~3-5s added to campaign creation.
  Setup: one env var (TAVILY_API_KEY or equivalent).
  Reliability: high — it's the standard approach.

  2. Meta Ad Library API

  Official Facebook Graph API endpoint. Free but requires a Meta developer app +
   access token.

  Reality check: requires FB dev setup and heavy rate limits. Not worth the pain
   vs. option 1 which covers Meta ads implicitly.

  3. Curated + refreshed database

  We manually maintain a "current winning UGC patterns" JSON updated monthly,
  based on our own research. Bakes into Sonnet's system prompt.

  Reality check: high-touch, doesn't scale, stales fast.

  My rec

  Go with #1 — web search API. Roughly:

  1. lib/trends/web-search.ts — thin wrapper around Tavily (I'd default to it —
  best free tier).
  2. When user hits "Plan campaign":
    - Auto-generate 3–4 queries from brand + product + goal (Sonnet writes them
  in a Haiku call — cheap and fast).
    - Fire the searches in parallel → 15–20 URLs back.
    - Fetch top 6 in parallel (same code we just shipped).
    - Feed to Sonnet planner as "current trending references".
  3. Show the user which sources fed the plan (transparency + trust — "Sources:
  6 pages fetched").

  Adds ~5s to planning. Costs ~$0.05 per campaign.

  One prereq: you'd need a Tavily API key in Vercel env (TAVILY_API_KEY). Free
  tier is 1000 searches/mo — plenty.

  Want me to build it? Confirm and I'll wire it up + tell you exactly where to
  paste the key.

  What just shipped

  - lib/trends/web-search.ts — Haiku 4.5 auto-writes 3–4 targeted queries from
  your brand + product + goal + audience → hits Tavily in parallel → dedupes +
  scores → returns top 8 sources.
  - /api/campaigns/plan now:
    a. Fetches trend/competitor sources automatically before Sonnet drafts the
  plan
    b. Feeds them to Sonnet as AUTO-DISCOVERED TREND & COMPETITOR SOURCES

  - /campaigns/[id] — collapsible "Sources (N)" block under the brief shows
  every URL Sonnet was fed, plus the query that surfaced it. Click through to
  the source.
  - Fails silently if the Tavily key isn't set — planner still runs on brand +
  brief.

  One thing you need to do

  Grab a Tavily API key (free tier is 1000 searches/mo, plenty):

  1. Go to https://tavily.com → sign up → dashboard → API keys → copy
  2. Add to Vercel:

  vercel env add TAVILY_API_KEY production
  # paste the key when prompted
  vercel env add TAVILY_API_KEY preview

  3. Redeploy (or wait for the next deploy — env vars pick up on next cold
  start).

  After that, every new campaign will auto-fetch 8 real trending references, and
   you'll see them listed under the campaign brief. Adds about 3–5s to campaign
  planning, costs ~$0 (free tier covers you).

  Existing campaigns won't have sources retroactively — only new ones after the
  key is set.

⏺ The prefill isn't landing because of two issues:
  1. My readCampaignShotPrefill removes the sessionStorage key on read, so React
   Strict Mode's double-render + Next's client hydration eats the value before
  the builder sees it.
  2. The consumed guard on the page prevents re-saving if the guard flag is
  stale from a previous visit.

  Making it robust — always write on landing, peek in the builder, only clear
  after render succeeds:

  Re: the Supabase egress

  Not alarming, but worth acting on. 7.87 GB out of 5 GB free tier for cached
  egress. This is bandwidth served from Supabase Storage — every time someone
  loads a generated video, product photo, or influencer portrait, it counts.
  Videos are the big ones (5–20 MB per MP4).

  What triggers it: anyone (including you during testing) loading /library,
  campaign pages, previews, or generated videos. Bots crawling public URLs.
  Video previews on shot cards.

  Options in order of ease:

  1. Upgrade to Supabase Pro ($25/mo) → 250 GB egress included. Simplest, and
  you probably need Pro anyway before launch (backups, larger DB, no
  auto-pause). Right move if you're heading toward users.
  2. Auto-upload rendered videos to Google Drive and swap the URL — Drive egress
   is free. Requires Drive plumbing (you have some already via the library
  integration).
  3. Cloudflare R2 — free egress, ~$0.015/GB storage. Requires moving the
  storage layer, bigger project.
  4. Do nothing — you don't get billed for overages on the Free plan, but
  Supabase may throttle you after some point. Restrictions kick in "gradually."

  My rec: upgrade to Pro now. Your app serves media as its whole thing — egress
  is your baseline cost, not a leak. Trying to engineer around $25/mo isn't the
  best use of your time pre-launch.

❯ Btw if we have the new campaign feature, should we remove the calendar thing  
  from the onboarding and add an option to create a campaign in the onboarding  
  ? what do you think, if you have another idea tell me                         

⏺ Yes, campaign wins — it's a much stronger "aha" than the calendar. Here's how
  I'd think about it:

  Why swap

  - Calendar is abstract: "here's a schedule of when to post" — doesn't have
  anything to click.
  - Campaign is concrete: 24 shots with real hooks, settings, scripts, credit
  totals — the user immediately sees the thing they're paying for.

  Campaign converts trials because it shows product value in 45 seconds.
  Calendar just shows a table of dates.

  What I'd actually build

  Two options — I'd pick B:

  A. Full campaign in onboarding
  Add campaign form as the final onboarding step. Pros: full wow. Cons: needs
  30-40s Sonnet call + slows first-run signup.

  B. Campaign lite → full ← my rec
  Onboarding generates a 6-shot preview (fast, ~10s Sonnet call, lightweight
  fields — hook + format + caption only). User sees the table right there in
  onboarding, feels the magic. On dashboard they get a "Expand to full 24-shot
  campaign" CTA that reruns the full planner. This gives the wow moment fast
  without gating signup on a long API call.

  Also — don't kill the calendar

  The calendar isn't useless, it's just wrong for onboarding. Keep it as a
  workspace feature — it becomes the scheduling layer for campaigns (drag
  rendered campaign shots onto dates → auto-post via Scheduler). That makes
  campaigns → calendar a natural downstream flow, not competing features.

  Other ideas worth considering

  - Onboarding = pick a format + generate one 8-second UGC. Even smaller
  commitment. Highest conversion but shows less of the product's actual scope.
  - Onboarding = pick a competitor URL, we analyze and generate the campaign —
  most impressive but fragile (competitor analysis was flaky).
  - Onboarding stays empty, dashboard has a big "Plan your first campaign" 
  prompt — lowest friction, but users bounce before seeing value.

  My verdict: ship B (6-shot campaign preview in onboarding, full expand on
  dashboard) + demote the monthly calendar to a workspace feature that consumes
  campaigns.

  Want me to build it? Say go and I'll wire it up.

  Re: Pinterest ad inspo for Product Studio

  Yes, technically possible but has trade-offs. Here's the honest read:

  Pinterest's official API — has an ads/pins endpoint but requires an approved
  business app + user OAuth. Their trust review is painful and gated to
  marketing partners. Not viable short-term.

  Scraping Pinterest — technically doable (pinterest.com/search/pins/?q=…) but
  Pinterest is aggressive about bot detection, blocks server-side IPs quickly,
  and rate-limits hard. Would work for a while, then break silently in prod.
  High-maintenance.

  Realistic paths that actually ship:

  1. Use the web-search API you already have (Tavily) with an image filter —
  Tavily can return image URLs from search results. Query: "{product category} 
  product photography ads 2026". You get a real spread across Pinterest,
  Behance, brand sites, ad libraries. Uses the same key you already added. This 
  is what I'd build.
  2. Google Custom Search Engine (Images) — free 100 queries/day, returns proper
   image URLs. Same idea, different API.
  3. Meta Ad Library API — free with a FB dev token; you can search competitor
  brands' image ads. Category-based search is limited, but brand-based search
  works.

  What "AI uses it as inspo" actually means

  Two implementation choices:

  - Style-transfer style: fetch 4-6 inspo images → feed them as referenceImages
  to Nano Banana alongside the user's product → NB Pro tries to match the visual
   style. This works well; NB Pro is trained for this.
  - Prompt-only: Sonnet reads inspo images (vision), writes a rich style prompt
  describing lighting/composition/color → passes that as text to NB. Cheaper,
  less accurate style match.

  My recommendation: wire Tavily image search + NB Pro reference-image pattern.
  It's the same infrastructure you already have. Adds ~$0.02 and ~4s per
  generation. Ships in a session.

  Want me to build it? Say go and I'll add "✨ Match a proven style" toggle to
  Product Studio that pulls 6 category-relevant ads and feeds them into the
  render.

  Shipped

  In Product Studio, new toggle: "✨ Match a proven style"

  Under the shoot area, right next to the aspect + count chips. When ON:

  1. Server infers the product's category (leverages your existing
  inferProductCategory from lib/multi-shot.ts).
  2. Tavily runs two targeted image searches — one for ad campaigns in that
  category, one for editorial product photography.
  3. Downloads up to 4 real reference images (Pinterest, Behance, brand sites,
  ad libraries — whatever surfaces).
  4. Feeds them to Nano Banana Pro alongside the product photos, with an
  explicit reference hint that says: "absorb the visual language — composition 
  energy, lighting, palette, negative-space instinct, typography treatment — but
   DO NOT copy their products/models/compositions."
  5. Returns inspoSources in the response (source URLs for what fed the shoot).

  Cost: ~$0.02 per shoot (2 Tavily searches). No extra credits charged to the
  user — same shoot price as before.

  Time: adds ~3–5s to the shoot start (parallel image fetch).

  Requires: TAVILY_API_KEY — already set for campaigns, no extra config needed.

  Fails silently if Tavily is unavailable or returns nothing → shoot just runs
  without inspo instead of erroring.

  Run a shoot with the toggle on for one of your existing products and see if
  the style shift lands. If NB is copying inspo too literally (or ignoring it),
  we can tune the hint wording.

❯ Whaat happens if i click ✨ Match a proven style and add an influencer with   
  it ?                                                                          

⏺ They coexist — the server passes both to NB Pro in the same shoot. Here's
  exactly what happens:

  Reference stack sent to NB Pro

  In this order:

  1. Style reference (if you uploaded one)
  2. Inspiration images — up to 4 real ads from Tavily
  3. Influencer identity refs — character sheet + portrait for each picked
  influencer (up to 6 total)
  4. Product photos — your hero product angles
  5. Co-products — additional products, one hero angle each

  Plus a reference hint that literally spells out which image is which and how
  NB should use each one.

  What NB does with it

  The hint on the inspo images says (verbatim):

  ▎ "Absorb their visual language: composition energy, lighting quality, colour 
  ▎ palette, texture, negative-space instinct, typography treatment. DO NOT copy
  ▎  any of their product, packaging, models, or specific compositions — just 
  ▎ channel the mood + polish."

  So the influencer's face + the product's design stay locked. The inspo
  controls lighting mood, palette, composition energy, typography vibe.

  The one real risk

  Face contamination. The inspo images almost certainly contain other
  people/models. Even with the "don't copy models" instruction, NB Pro can
  occasionally blend features from inspo faces into your influencer's face —
  especially if the inspo has similar-looking models. NB Pro is pretty good at
  this because the identity refs come right before the product refs (higher
  salience), but it's not bulletproof.

  What to try

  Run a shoot with your favorite influencer + a product + Match a proven style
  ON. Look at the resulting faces vs. the influencer's canonical portrait. If
  they drift, tell me and I'll do one of:

  1. Auto-skip inspo when an influencer is picked — cleanest, keeps identity
  guarantee
  2. Face-mask the inspo images — draw a rectangle over any faces server-side
  before passing to NB
  3. Stronger prompt language — usually the weakest fix but easiest

  My hunch: it'll be fine 8/10 times, weird 2/10. Ship it, test, adjust. Want me
   to also add a UI hint on the toggle saying "⚠️ May slightly blend inspo faces
   with your influencer" to set expectations?
